newsitem.title: USA: Judge refuses to stay order on Simpson children.
newsitem.headline: Judge refuses to stay order on Simpson children.

text.p: A judge Friday refused to stay her order awarding O.J. Simpson custody of the two young children he had with his slain ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson.

"She doesn't have a heart," Nicole Brown Simpson's sister Denise said of Orange County Superior Court Judge Nancy Wieben Stock. "I'm just livid," she told reporters outside the courthouse in Fullerton, some 50 miles south of Los Angeles.
But the court-appointed lawyer for the children, Marjorie Fuller, who has visited them since they have been with Simpson, said: "The children are happy to be with their father."
The hearing was held behind closed doors and there was no official announcement of the judge's ruling. Stock herself refused to comment.
The Brown family had gone to court requesting Judge Stock stay her December order -- pending the family's appeal -- giving the ex-football star custody of Sydney, 11, and her brother Justin, 8.
The children lived with their maternal grandparents since their father was arrested in June 1994 on suspicion of murdering their mother and her friend Ronald Goldman.

Simpson was acquitted of the murders by a criminal jury in October 1995, but the children remained with their grandparents until Judge Stock's ruling last year. They have since moved back to their father's mansion in Los Angeles.
Simpson is currently awaiting a jury's verdict in a wrongful death civil suit brought by the victims' families.
Commenting on the judge's decision Friday, Brown family attorney Natasha Roit said: "It was not expected."
But the children's attorney Fuller told reporters the only question Judge Stock had to ask was: "Is O.J. Simpson a better parent than the Browns?"

"Is O.J. Simpson such a terrible parent that it would be detrimental to his children to allow them to live with him and is it essential to the children's welfare that they must be removed from his custody?
"If you can't answer that question with a 'yes', then under our laws, he's entitled to raise his children, even if there are many people in the world who would be better parents," Fuller said.
